name: Haa
tagline: A quiet valley over Chele La, opened to tourists only in 2002
meta_description: Haa valley, Bhutan: the White and Black temples, farmhouse stays, hoentoe, the July summer festival, the Chele La drive, permits and 2026 costs.
summary: Haa is a high, quiet valley in western Bhutan, with its town at about 2,720 m, reached from Paro over Chele La in 2.5–3 hours. It opened to foreign tourists only in 2002. Come for the White and Black temples, farmhouse stays, buckwheat hoentoe and the July festival. You need a route permit and a licensed guide.
intro: Haa sits in the far west of Bhutan, a long valley of barley and buckwheat fields, blue pine and old farmhouses along the Haa Chhu. The town, Haa-Namjayling, stands at about 2,720 m, so it is a few degrees colder than Paro all year. The district borders Tibet and covers about 1,905 sq km with fewer than 14,000 people, which makes it the second least populated district after Gasa. Most visitors arrive over Chele La, the 3,988 m pass on the road from Paro, and drop down through forest into a valley that still feels like a working farm community.

Haa was closed to foreign tourists until 2002, when the valley was opened after the 79th session of the National Assembly. That late start shows. There are no hotel strips, few souvenir shops and very little traffic. The Indian Military Training Team, IMTRAT, has a long-standing base here, training the Royal Bhutan Army and the Royal Bodyguard, so you will see neat camps and soldiers near the town. Close by stands Wangchuck Lhodzong, the district's dzong, and less than a kilometre to its south is Lhakhang Karpo, the White Temple, which local historians date to the 7th century.

We send people to Haa for slow days rather than a list of sights. Sleep in a registered farmhouse, take a hot stone bath, eat hoentoe, the buckwheat dumplings the valley is known for, and walk between villages with your guide. Two nights is right for most trips; one night works if you are short of time, and a day trip from Paro is possible but rushed. Haa needs a route permit on top of the standard Thimphu–Paro entry permit, and you must travel with a licensed guide. Your operator arranges both. Rules are being revised, so check current status before you travel.

story.title: Two pigeons, two temples
paras: The best-known story in Haa is about its two old temples, and it is a legend, told in several ways. One version says that a white pigeon and a black pigeon, emanations of the Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo, who ruled in the 7th century, flew south from Tibet and came down in this valley. Where the white bird landed, people built Lhakhang Karpo, the White Temple. Where the black bird landed, they built Lhakhang Nagpo, the Black Temple. Another version replaces the birds with rays of light, bright and dark, that streamed from the king's body to mark the two sites.

A third telling says the temples were built by three groups of people who came out of the three hills above the valley, known as Miri Phünsum, the 'three brother' hills. Local historians date both temples to the 7th century, the same period that tradition gives Kyichu Lhakhang in Paro. Lhakhang Karpo was extensively restored and partly rebuilt around 2011, so much of what you see is recent work on a very old site. Lhakhang Nagpo, a short distance away, is smaller and quieter, and holds a small pool associated with Mahakala, the protector deity.

Haa has a modern story too. Gongzim Ugyen Dorji, the first chief minister under King Ugyen Wangchuck and the man who ran Bhutan's affairs from Bhutan House in Kalimpong, was also Penlop, or governor, of Haa from 1907 to 1916. His grandson Jigme Palden Dorji, later Bhutan's first prime minister, was appointed administrator of Haa in 1928, when he was nine years old. Ask your guide about the Dorji family's place in the valley's memory; it is one of the threads that ties Haa to the Darjeeling and Kalimpong hills.
story.source: Haa District and Uesu Gewog articles (Wikipedia), citing local histories; Haa Dzongkhag Administration; biographies of Ugyen Dorji and Jigme Palden Dorji

did_you_know: Haa was opened to foreign tourists only in 2002, after the 79th session of Bhutan's National Assembly.
Gongzim Ugyen Dorji, Bhutan's first chief minister, was also governor (Penlop) of Haa from 1907 to 1916.
The Indian Military Training Team (IMTRAT), based in Haa, trains personnel of the Royal Bhutan Army and the Royal Bodyguard of Bhutan.
facts: White and Black temples, farmhouse stays, hoentoe, July festival

highlights.title: Lhakhang Karpo and Lhakhang Nagpo
highlights.text: The White and Black temples, which local historians date to the 7th century, sit a short distance apart at the edge of town. Go in the morning, walk clockwise, keep long sleeves on, and ask your guide to tell the pigeon legend in front of the three hills it points to.

highlights.title: Chele La on the way in
highlights.text: The road from Paro climbs to 3,988 m at Chele La, with long strings of prayer flags and, on clear mornings, Jomolhari to the north. Leave Paro by 7 am for the best chance of a view, then drop 26 km down through forest into the Haa valley.

highlights.title: A night in a farmhouse
highlights.text: Registered farmhouse homestays in the villages give you a wooden room, home cooking and often a dotsho, a hot stone bath in which river stones heated in a fire are dropped into a wooden tub. It is the most Haa thing you can do, and often cheaper than a hotel.

highlights.title: Hoentoe, the Haa dumpling
highlights.text: Hoentoe are buckwheat dumplings filled with dried turnip leaves, cheese and butter, and they are the dish Haa is known for. Ask your homestay a day ahead and they will often make a batch; it takes hours, so do not expect them on demand in town restaurants.

highlights.title: The Haa Summer Festival
highlights.text: Held every July, the festival celebrates the valley's farming and herding life, with local food, songs, dances and traditional games. Dates change each year and the monsoon brings cloud, but the valley is at its greenest and alpine flowers are out on the high slopes.

highlights.title: Walks between villages
highlights.text: With your guide you can walk easy farm tracks between villages, along the Haa Chhu, or up to small temples such as Katsho Goenpa. Paths are mostly gentle, but you are at 2,700 m, so go slowly on the first day if you came straight from the plains.

how_to_reach.text: From Paro, a Bhutan-registered tourist car with driver takes 2.5–3 hours over Chele La (≈ 65–70 km). From Thimphu, allow about 4 hours. A lower road from Chhuzom, the river confluence on the Thimphu–Phuentsholing highway, is used when snow closes the pass. Expect ₹4,500–6,500 a day for the car, indicative, 2026; check current status before you travel.

Your operator gets the route permit for Haa from the Immigration office in Thimphu on a working day (Mon–Fri) and provides a licensed guide, who is mandatory beyond the first checkpoint under the Department of Tourism notification of 8 April 2026. Build that working day into your plan, and check current status before you travel.

Fly into Paro from Delhi, Kolkata or, seasonally, Bagdogra on Drukair or Bhutan Airlines, then drive to Haa the same or next day. Overland, take the train to NJP or Hasimara, enter Bhutan at Phuentsholing, and reach Haa via Thimphu or Paro over two days.

where_to_stay: Haa has a handful of Department of Tourism-certified hotels in and around Haa town, mostly small 3-star properties with wood stoves or heaters, and a growing list of registered farmhouse homestays in the villages up and down the valley. We usually book a farmhouse for at least one night: rooms are simple and bathrooms can be basic or shared, but the food and the hot stone bath make up for it. Hotels suit families who want attached bathrooms and steady hot water. There are no luxury lodges in the valley, so premium travellers often stay in Paro and come for the day. Ask your operator for the current certified list, since only listed stays are allowed.
costs: ₹1,200 per person per night; US$100 for most other nationalities, check current status before you travel
Hot stone bath at a farmhouse
₹3,000–5,500 per room night with breakfast, indicative, 2026
budget_tip: Spend your Haa night in a registered farmhouse with dinner and breakfast included; it usually costs less than a 3-star room plus restaurant meals, and the food is better.
tips: Carry warm layers even in May and October; Haa at 2,720 m gets close to freezing at night, and Chele La is colder still.
Carry cash in ₹500 or smaller notes; card and UPI acceptance in Haa is patchy and ATMs can be offline.
Route permits are issued on working days, so let your operator plan the Haa leg around weekends and public holidays.
Wear long sleeves and long trousers or a skirt for the temples, take off caps, and do not photograph inside the shrine rooms.
Do not photograph the IMTRAT or army camps, gates or sentries; ask your guide where photos are fine.

experiences.title: Haa's White and Black temples
experiences.cost: Free or a small fee; offerings welcome, check current status before you travel
experiences.summary: A short morning visit to the two oldest temples in Haa, the White Temple and the Black Temple, which local historians date to the 7th century. Your guide tells the pigeon legend, you walk the courtyards clockwise, and you see the three hills the stories point to.
body: Lhakhang Karpo, the White Temple, stands less than a kilometre south of Wangchuck Lhodzong at the edge of Haa town. It is the larger of the two, with whitewashed walls, a wide courtyard and a backdrop of three forested hills, Miri Phünsum, the 'three brothers'. The temple was extensively restored and partly rebuilt around 2011, so the paint and woodwork look newer than the site's age. Local historians date its founding to the 7th century, in the reign of the Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo, the same period tradition gives Kyichu Lhakhang in Paro.

Lhakhang Nagpo, the Black Temple, is a short distance away. It is smaller and quieter, and inside is a small pool associated with Mahakala, the protector deity. The legend that links the two is told in several ways: a white pigeon and a black pigeon, emanations of Songtsen Gampo, flew here from Tibet and landed where the temples now stand; or bright and dark rays of light marked the spots. Treat these as legends, and ask your guide which version his or her family tells.

Visit in the morning, when butter lamps are being lit and caretakers are about. Wear long sleeves and long trousers or a skirt, take off caps and shoes where asked, and do not photograph inside the shrine rooms. Walk around both temples clockwise. Both are working places of worship, so if a ritual is under way, wait quietly at the back or come back later. Combine the visit with a slow walk through town and past the dzong for a gentle first half-day after the Chele La drive.

faqs.q: How old are the White and Black temples of Haa
faqs.a: Local historians date both to the 7th century, during the reign of the Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo, the same period tradition gives Kyichu Lhakhang in Paro. That date rests on tradition rather than surviving records. Lhakhang Karpo was extensively restored and partly rebuilt around 2011, so much of what you see is recent work on an ancient site.

faqs.q: Can tourists go inside Lhakhang Karpo
faqs.a: Usually yes, with your licensed guide, when the caretaker is present and no private ritual is under way. Dress with long sleeves and long trousers or a skirt, remove your cap, and keep cameras in the bag inside the shrine rooms. Courtyard photos are generally fine. Opening hours are informal, so mornings are the safest time to go.

faqs.q: How far are the temples from Haa town
faqs.a: Lhakhang Karpo is less than a kilometre south of Wangchuck Lhodzong, at the edge of Haa town, so most people walk or take a two-minute drive. Lhakhang Nagpo is a short distance further. Allow 1.5–2 hours for both, with time to sit, listen to the legends and look at the three hills above the valley.

experiences.title: A farmhouse night with hoentoe
experiences.cost: ₹2,000–4,000 per person with meals; hot stone bath ₹1,500–3,000, indicative, 2026
experiences.summary: Spend a night with a farming family in a registered Haa homestay: a wooden house, a wood stove, red rice and ema datshi, a hot stone bath, and, if you ask a day ahead, a tray of hoentoe, the buckwheat dumplings the valley is known for.
body: Haa farmhouses are usually two or three storeys of stone or rammed earth and timber, with the family living upstairs, a prayer room with an altar, and stores below. Registered homestays are the only private homes tourists may stay in, so your operator books from the official list. Rooms are simple: a bed or floor mattress, thick quilts, a heater or wood stove. Bathrooms may be shared and hot water may come in a bucket. That is part of the deal, and we tell people so before they book.

The food is the reason to come. Expect red rice, ema datshi (chillies in cheese), a vegetable or two from the garden, and suja, salted butter tea. Hoentoe are the Haa speciality: buckwheat dough wrapped around a filling of dried turnip leaves, cheese and butter, then steamed or fried. Making them takes a few hours, so ask your guide to request them a day ahead. Families make them for celebrations, including Lomba, the winter new year that Haa and Paro keep by the lunar calendar.

Most farmhouses can also prepare a dotsho, a hot stone bath. River stones are heated in a fire for hours, then dropped into a wooden tub of water, often with herbs added; the stones hiss and the water heats slowly. It costs extra, usually ₹1,500–3,000, indicative, 2026, and needs ordering by early afternoon. After a cold day on Chele La, it is the best money you will spend in Haa. Settle the bill through your operator or directly as agreed, and carry small notes.

faqs.q: What is hoentoe
faqs.a: Hoentoe is a buckwheat dumpling from Haa, filled with dried turnip leaves, cheese and butter, then steamed or fried. It is the valley's signature dish and is made in homes for celebrations such as Lomba, the local winter new year. Restaurants rarely keep it ready, so ask your homestay or guide to arrange it a day ahead.

faqs.q: Are Haa homestays safe and clean
faqs.a: Registered farmhouse homestays are listed with the tourism authorities, and tourists may only stay in listed ones, so standards are basic but known. Expect clean quilts, simple rooms and sometimes shared bathrooms. Ask your operator for photos of the room and bathroom before you book, and request one with an attached toilet if that matters to you.

faqs.q: How much does a hot stone bath cost in Haa
faqs.a: Expect about ₹1,500–3,000 per bath, indicative, 2026, depending on the farmhouse and how many people share the tub. The stones need several hours in the fire, so order it by early afternoon. Skip it if you have heart problems or high blood pressure, and do not drink ara before getting in.

experiences.title: Haa Summer Festival in July
experiences.cost: Free to watch; usual SDF, guide and car costs apply
experiences.summary: Each July Haa holds a summer festival that celebrates the valley's farming and herding life, with local dishes, songs, dances and traditional games. It falls in the monsoon, so pack rain gear, but the valley is green and the high slopes are in flower.
body: Unlike the big tshechus, which are religious festivals of masked dances held in dzong courtyards, the Haa Summer Festival is a celebration of the valley's way of life. It is held every July, with recent editions in mid-July, and runs over a few days. Expect food stalls with Haa dishes such as hoentoe, local cheese and ara, folk songs and dances, traditional sports and games, and displays about the herding families who spend summers with their animals in the high pastures.

July is the monsoon in Bhutan, so the festival is a deliberate choice: the fields are green, flowers are out on the high slopes, and Haa itself records about 880 mm of rain a year, far less than southern Bhutan. Chele La can be in cloud and roads can be slow after heavy rain, so leave Paro early and allow extra time. Landslides occasionally close roads in the monsoon; check current status before you travel.

Dates are announced each year by the organisers and the Department of Tourism, sometimes only a few months ahead, so confirm them before you book flights. Hotels and farmhouses in Haa are few, and festival nights fill first; book early, or stay in Paro and come for the day. Watch from the edges, ask before photographing people, and dress modestly in long sleeves and long trousers or a skirt, as you would anywhere in rural Bhutan.

faqs.q: When is the Haa Summer Festival
faqs.a: It is held every July. Exact dates change each year and are announced by the organisers and Bhutan's Department of Tourism; recent editions have fallen in mid-July. Confirm the dates before booking flights or hotels, and check current status before you travel, as monsoon weather can affect roads and events.

faqs.q: Do I need a ticket for the Haa Summer Festival
faqs.a: We are not aware of a separate ticket for visitors; the festival is generally free to watch. You still pay the Sustainable Development Fee for each night in Bhutan, and you need a route permit for Haa and a licensed guide, which your operator arranges. Stalls charge for food and crafts, so carry small notes.

faqs.q: Is July a good time to visit Haa
faqs.a: It is good for the festival, green fields and flowers, but it is the monsoon, so expect cloud on Chele La and some rain. Haa is drier than southern Bhutan, at about 880 mm of rain a year. For clear mountain views, come in April–May or October–November instead.

experiences.title: A slow walk through Haa town
experiences.summary: An easy two-hour walk with your guide through Haa town: the small bazaar, the outside of Wangchuck Lhodzong, the river and the edge of the army cantonment, ending at a tea shop. It is the best way to see how this border valley lives today.
body: Haa town, officially Haa-Namjayling, is small enough to walk in an hour. The bazaar is a short stretch of painted two- and three-storey shophouses with general stores, a few restaurants and district offices. Most shops sell everyday goods to local families rather than souvenirs, which is part of the appeal. Prices are in ngultrum, which is equal to the rupee, and Indian notes of ₹500 and below are accepted. Stop for suja or sweet milk tea and watch the town go about its day.

Wangchuck Lhodzong is the district's dzong, a small fortress near the IMTRAT camp. The Indian Military Training Team has been in Haa for decades; it is described as the oldest training team India has sent to a friendly foreign country, and it trains personnel of the Royal Bhutan Army and the Royal Bodyguard. That gives the town an orderly feel and a small Indian presence. Do not photograph military areas, and ask your guide before you point a camera at any gate or sentry.

Haa is also tied to one of Bhutan's best-known families. Gongzim Ugyen Dorji, the first chief minister under King Ugyen Wangchuck, was Penlop, or governor, of Haa from 1907 to 1916, and his grandson Jigme Palden Dorji, later Bhutan's first prime minister, was made administrator of Haa in 1928 at the age of nine. End the walk by the Haa Chhu at dusk, when cattle come home and the temperature drops fast.

faqs.q: Is Haa town worth a visit or just the valley
faqs.a: The town itself is small and plain, with a short bazaar, the district dzong and an army camp, and that is the point: it shows a working Bhutanese valley town rather than a tourist strip. Give it two hours on foot, then spend the rest of your time in the temples, villages and farmhouses around it.

faqs.q: Can I take photos in Haa town
faqs.a: Yes, in the bazaar and of the landscape. Do not photograph the IMTRAT or Royal Bhutan Army camps, gates or soldiers, and do not fly a drone without prior permission. Ask before photographing people, especially monks and elders. Inside temples and the dzong's shrine rooms, photography is not allowed.

faqs.q: Is there an ATM in Haa
faqs.a: There are bank branches in Haa town, but ATMs can be offline and cards are not always accepted. Carry enough cash from Paro or Thimphu for your stay, in ₹500 or smaller notes, which are accepted alongside ngultrum. UPI works in some shops, but do not rely on it.

faqs.q: Do Indians need a permit to visit Haa
faqs.a: Yes. Indian nationals need the free Entry Permit, which covers Thimphu and Paro, plus a route permit for Haa, issued by the Immigration office in Thimphu on working days. In practice your Bhutanese operator or guide gets it for you. Reports suggest the process is being simplified, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is a guide compulsory in Haa for Indian tourists
faqs.a: Plan on it. A Department of Tourism notification of 8 April 2026 says all tourists must be accompanied by a licensed guide beyond the first designated checkpoint, and we read this as covering Indian visitors too. Older advice that Indians can travel without a guide is out of date. Plan on a licensed guide for the whole trip beyond Phuentsholing, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Haa from Paro
faqs.a: About 65–70 km over Chele La, which takes 2.5–3 hours by car with a stop at the pass. Chele La is about 35 km from Paro and 26 km from Haa. In winter, snow can close the pass for a day or more, and a longer road via Chhuzom is used instead. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I do Haa as a day trip from Paro
faqs.a: You can, but it is a long day: 5–6 hours of driving for the round trip, plus the pass and the temples, and you still need the route permit. We prefer at least one night in a Haa farmhouse, which gives you an unhurried evening, the hot stone bath and a clear morning on Chele La on the way back.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Haa
faqs.a: April–May and October–November are best, with mostly dry days and the clearest views from Chele La. July brings the summer festival and green fields but also monsoon cloud. December–February is very cold, with a recorded low of −14.5 °C, and snow can close Chele La. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much does a Haa trip cost for Indians
faqs.a: As a couple sharing a car and guide, a 2-night Haa add-on to a Paro trip costs roughly ₹13,000–20,000 per person, indicative, 2026. That covers the ₹1,200 SDF per night, a farmhouse or 3-star room, and your share of the car (₹4,500–6,500 a day) and guide (₹2,000–3,000 a day). Groups of four pay noticeably less each.

faqs.q: What is special about Haa
faqs.a: Haa opened to foreign tourists only in 2002, so it has few hotels, little traffic and a farming life that carries on regardless of visitors. It has the White and Black temples, dated by local tradition to the 7th century, the hoentoe dumpling, farmhouse stays and the drive over Chele La. Come for slow days rather than a list of sights.

faqs.q: Is Haa cold
faqs.a: Yes, colder than Paro. The town is at about 2,720 m and the record low is −14.5 °C, set in January. Even in May and October, nights drop to a few degrees above freezing, and Chele La on the way is colder and windy. Pack a down jacket, a warm hat and thermal layers, and ask for a room with a heater.

faqs.q: Where do you stay in Haa
faqs.a: In a Department of Tourism-certified 3-star hotel in Haa town or a registered farmhouse homestay in the villages around it. There are no luxury lodges in the valley. Farmhouses have simpler bathrooms but better food and the hot stone bath; hotels have attached bathrooms and steadier hot water. Ask your operator for the current certified list.
